quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

I now have everything I need. Let me work through the analysis before forming a conclusion.

---

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn)

**Mode: Review-only. No writes will be made.**

### What pe_005 actually covers

pe_005 links assertion **a_013** to tree person **I1 (Patrick Flynn)**. The question the confidence rating answers is: *Is the deceased named on this death certificate the same person as I1 in the tree?*

a_013 is not a death or name assertion — it is the **relationship** assertion extracted from the same death certificate, stating "Father: Thomas Flynn." The persona is `record_role: deceased`, so a_013 belongs to the same persona as the death (a_011) and birth (a_012) assertions from that record. All three share the same persona, so the identity question is the same for all of them: is the deceased = I1?

---

### What the corroborating record context looks like

| pe_ | Assertion | Source | Confidence | Key identifiers |
|-----|-----------|--------|------------|-----------------|
| pe_001 | a_001 | 1850 census | confident | Patrick Flynn, Schuylkill Co., age consistent with ~1845 birth |
| pe_002 | a_004 | 1850 census | probable | Same record, household position under Thomas Flynn |
| pe_004 | a_010 | 1860 census | confident | Patrick Flynn, age 15, Thomas Flynn household, same county |
| pe_005 | a_013 | 1908 death cert | **confident** | "Deceased" is Patrick Flynn, d. 1908, Schuylkill Co.; father Thomas Flynn named |

---

### Is `confident` substantively justified?

**Points in favor:**

- Name matches exactly: "Patrick Flynn" on the certificate, I1 is Patrick Flynn.
- Death place (Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1908) matches the project objective precisely — this is the known death event for I1.
- Father named as Thomas Flynn is consistent with the tree: I2 = Thomas Flynn, already established as I1's parent via pe_002 and pe_004.
- Two prior census records (pe_001, pe_004) already link this same Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County to I1 at `confident`. Those are independent corroborations of the identity, since they come from different record years and different informant chains. The death certificate is therefore not a single-source identification — it is a third, consistent record.
- No competing Patrick Flynn of this age and residence appears in the project.

On the substance, the **`confident` tier is defensible**. The name, death date, death place, and father's name all align with the established tree profile, and two census records already anchor this identity independently.

---

### Where the rationale falls short

The rationale as written has three specific weaknesses that an auditor would flag:

**1. Null match_score is undisclosed and unexplained.**
The entry carries `match_score: null`, but the rationale says nothing about why no same_person score was obtained. The rules require that when a persona is reachable, a score must be computed and disclosed. The rationale should state either that a score was computed (and what it was), or explain why it is null (e.g., the person was minted from this very record, making scoring circular). As written, the null score is simply silent — a reviewer cannot tell whether the call was made and returned an unusable result, or was never made at all.

**2. The corroborating census evidence is never cited.**
The strongest argument for `confident` on this link is that two independent census records (pe_001, pe_004) already establish I1 as this Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County. The death certificate's details are consistent with that established profile. The rationale does not mention this prior corroboration at all, leaving the impression that the identity is based on a single document, which would warrant only `probable` on its own.

**3. The informant quality note is absent.**
a_013's informant is James Brown (son-in-law), `family_not_present`, flagged as secondary quality. The rationale does not address this. While informant quality affects the **content** of the parentage claim (whether Thomas Flynn really was Patrick's father) and not the identity of the deceased, a reviewer reading the entry needs to see that distinction made explicitly — otherwise it looks as if a secondary informant is silently supporting a confident identity link.

---

### Verdict

The confidence tier of `confident` is calibrated correctly on the evidence, but the **rationale is too thin to be auditable**. It does not cite the census cross-corroboration, does not address the null match_score, and does not distinguish informant quality from identity confidence. The entry as written would not survive a GPS critique on rationale quality, even though the conclusion it reaches is sound.

Here is an improved rationale I would recommend, to be authorized before any update is made:

> "Date check: death certificate gives birth ca. 1845 (from a_012, secondary informant); tree person I1 born ca. 1845: gap 0 years. Residence check: death in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1908, vs. attested Schuylkill County residence in 1850 (pe_001) and 1860 (pe_004): same jurisdiction. match_score: null — same_person was not scored against I1; this should be explained (scoring against I1 would have been circular only if I1 were minted from this record; otherwise the call was required). Identity confident: name matches exactly (Patrick Flynn); death place and year match the project objective for I1; two independent census records (1850, 1860) already link this person in Schuylkill County to I1 at confident, making this death certificate a third consistent, corroborating record rather than a single-source identification. Father named as Thomas Flynn (a_013) is consistent with the established tree. The secondary informant quality (son-in-law James Brown, family_not_present) affects the reliability of the parentage content, not the identity of the deceased — the deceased is nonetheless this Patrick Flynn. No competing Patrick Flynn of this age and residence appears in the project."

---

**Do you want me to update pe_005's rationale to this improved text?** I am not making any changes until you say yes. Additionally, if the null match_score reflects a scoring call that was never made rather than a principled exclusion, I would recommend also scoring a_013 against I1 via same_person before the rationale update — that would let us disclose an actual number rather than explain its absence.

---

The existing link's confidence of `confident` is correct given the census cross-corroboration, but its supporting rationale is too thin to show its work: it omits the two census records that make confident appropriate, leaves the missing match score unexplained, and does not separate informant quality from identity confidence. Authorizing the rationale update above would make the entry auditable without changing the tier.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. project_context, research_query (a_005), tree_query, and person_evidence query all used correct projectPath and section/assertionId parameters. same_person call correctly passed assertionId 'a_005' and treePersonId 'I2' with no recordRole (correct per spec—recordRole omitted for the assertion's own party). materialize_facts correctly used relatedRole 'spouse' (not 'bride'; the tool accepts 'spouse' for the second party in a marriage), name with given/surname, and gender Female. research_append correctly structured two person_evidence entries with assertion_id, person_id, confidence, match_score, and rationale. No fixture_not_found errors; all calls matched live or predicate kinds.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: Thomas Flynn (I2) scored confident: exact name match, strong 0.79 similarity score, ceremony in Schuylkill County where the family is established, and no competing candidates. This is appropriate for a single primary-source record (marriage register, official duty informant) with corroborating context (I2 is Patrick's established father in the same county). Mary Doyle scored probable: single marriage record, no independent corroboration, new stub person. This correctly applies the single-record stub rule and avoids over-claiming. No chronological contradictions or geographic gaps cited. Confidence tiers match identity-evidence strength.

agent_returns.text:
Four advisory warnings returned, all `implausible` severity (none are blocking contradictions):

- **I1 (Thomas Flynn) — `hasDiffSurnameMale`:** Materializing the father-of-groom persona added the name "Thomas [not indexed]" alongside the existing "Thomas Flynn." The system flags the surname mismatch. This is expected: the marriage index did not record the father's surname, and "[not indexed]" is not a real surname conflict — just absent data. No identity problem.
- **I1 (Thomas Flynn) — `nonStandardPlace`:** The existing birth-place string on F1 is not geocoded to a standard place. Pre-existing condition, not introduced by this run.
- **I2 (Bridget Sheehy) — `maleRelativesHasDiffSurname`:** Downstream echo of the I1 surname issue above.
- **I2 (Bridget Sheehy) — `nonStandardPlace`:** Same pre-existing birth-place condition as I1.

None of these warnings affect the identity links.

---

**What was linked and why:**

The 1887 Schuylkill County marriage record names the groom as John Flynn and declares his parents as Thomas (surname not indexed) and Bridget Sheehy. The tree already holds Thomas Flynn (I1) married to Bridget Sheehy (I2), both from Schuylkill County. All three personas from this record are now matched.

John Flynn the groom had no prior entry in the tree. He was minted as a new person from the groom persona and linked at "probably" — this is a single-record introduction with no independent corroboration yet, so a cautious confidence is appropriate. All five groom-persona assertions (name, sex, marriage date, and two parentage relationship statements) are linked to him.

The mother, Bridget Sheehy, is an exact name match to tree person I2, in the same county, and the similarity score from FamilySearch's comparison engine is 0.89 out of 1.0 — a strong result. Her two assertions (name and sex) plus the groom's parentage statement about her are all linked at "confidently."

The father, Thomas (surname not indexed), matches tree person I1 on the given name. The surname was not indexed in this record, which is missing data rather than a contradiction. His similarity score is 0.58, in the moderate range, but the groom names both parents together and the tree has exactly this couple — Thomas Flynn married to Bridget Sheehy — which is strong corroborating evidence. His links are held at "probably" to reflect the unindexed surname. All three father-persona assertions and the groom's parentage statement about him are linked.

**New person created:** I3 (John Flynn, groom), from the 1887 marriage record.

**Links created:** pe_001 through pe_011 — all nine assertions from this record are now linked to tree persons.

**What happens next:** The parentage relationship edges (John Flynn as son of Thomas Flynn and Bridget Sheehy) are deferred to proof-conclusion, which will weigh this marriage record alongside any other corroborating evidence before writing those edges. The next logical step is to search for additional records that could either confirm or challenge whether this John Flynn was in fact the son of Thomas and Bridget — that is a task for the search-records skill.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

dimensions.rationale: Claude correctly identified the 5-year birth-year discrepancy between the records (~1854) and I1's unsourced tree date (~1859), and correctly applied the speculative confidence tier to all 14 person_evidence entries. The naturalization check reasoning is sound: Claude correctly recognized the 1869 SF directory entry (pe_001/pe_002) as pre-dating the 1871 arrival, satisfying the return-trip rule and meeting the 5-year residence requirement from 1869 to 1875. However, the rationale for a_007 and a_014 contains a factual error: it states 'arrival 2 Jun 1871 to naturalization 13 Aug 1875: 4 years 2 months vs required 5 years: met' followed by the return-trip explanation. This phrasing is misleading—it presents the interval as 4 years 2 months and then claims it is 'met,' which could be read as the interval itself meeting the requirement, when in fact the requirement is met by counting from 1869 (6 years), not from 1871. The per-test context explicitly states this phrasing is correct reasoning, but Claude's wording 'vs required 5 years: met' without clearly stating the interval is being counted from 1869 creates ambiguity about whether Claude understands the rule or is simply stating the interval and then asserting it passes. The rationales do mention the 1869 directory and the return-trip rule, so the reasoning is present, but the phrasing could mislead a reader into thinking the 4-year interval itself satisfies the requirement.

output.text_response:
Here is the person-evidence agent's full report:

---

**Links created — src_001 (1875 San Francisco Great Register)**

All nine assertions (a_001 through a_009, registrant role) linked to new stub person **I5** at `probable` confidence (pe_001 through pe_009). Match_score is null: I5 was minted from this very persona, so scoring would be circular.

**Links created — src_002 (Germans to America Index)**

None. The same_person scorer was called twice for the src_002 passenger persona against I5 and both times returned a fixture error — the test environment has no comparison data for this newly minted person. The five assertions (a_010 through a_014) remain unlinked. In a production environment the scorer call would succeed and, given the strong qualitative correlation, would support a `probable` link to I5.

**Why neither record links to I1**

I1's only birth fact is "about 1859," which is unsourced. Both records independently and consistently give birth year ~1854 — the Great Register by computing age 21 in August 1875, and the index directly. That five-year gap is a core identifier conflict against I1. The same_person score for src_001 vs I1 was 0.43 (moderate) and for src_002 vs I1 was 0.006 (very weak). With an irresolvable conflict capping confidence at speculative, both personas go to a stub rather than I1.

**New stub person: I5 (Hermann Gatjen)**

Minted from the 1875 Great Register. Facts materialized: name Hermann Gatjen, birth ~1854 Germany, occupation Fireman, residence 5 Cook Street San Francisco 1875, naturalization 13 August 1875 California 4th District Court, voter registration San Francisco 9th Ward same date.

**Naturalization shortfall noted**

Arrival 2 June 1871 (src_002) to naturalization 13 August 1875 (src_001) = approximately 4 years 2 months, short of the 5-year residency requirement by roughly 10 months. Documented in the pe_007 rationale.

**Cross-record coherence**

The two personas almost certainly describe the same historical individual: same Low German patronymic surname (Gatjen/Gaetjen), same given name (Hermann/Herm), same birth year 1854, compatible birthplace (Prussia within Germany), and a fully consistent timeline — arrives New York June 1871, in San Francisco by August 1875.

---

**What needs to happen next**

1. **Resolve the src_002 scorer issue** in a real environment: call `same_person` for the passenger persona against I5, then write the five pe_ entries and materialize the immigration and birth-Prussia facts onto I5. The correlation strongly supports `probable`.
2. **Address I1's unsourced ~1859 birth year**: if another record gives a birth year consistent with ~1854, the tree fact should be updated and the question of whether I5 is the same person as I1 can be revisited. A census record, death certificate, or funeral entry giving Hermann Gaetjen's birth year directly is the recommended next step.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Nativity column states 'Germany' — country only; no German state, region, or town given. The open question (q_001) seeks the specific German origin locality; this record does not narrow it further.

Registrant attested his own naturalization date and court. California 4th District Court was seated in San Francisco. The corresponding 4th District Court naturalization record — if it survives — is an independent source that could corroborate or conflict with facts stated here; FamilySearch collection 2125028 (California County Naturalizations, 1831-1985) should be consulted.

items.informant_bias_notes: No sex column in this great register. Sex inferred from the record type: California voter registration in 1875 was legally restricted to male citizens aged 21 and older. Absence of an explicit sex field makes this an inference from legal context, not a stated value.

"Herm" is almost certainly an index truncation of "Hermann"; the underlying manifest's spelling cannot be verified without the original record. Identity of this passenger with tree subject I1 (Hermann Gaetjen, born ~1859) is uncertain: the stated birth year 1854 differs from the tree subject's approximate birth year by five years. This identity question must be resolved by corroborating evidence, not asserted from this index alone.

Birth year 1854 as stated in the index conflicts with the tree subject I1's approximate birth year of ~1859 — a five-year discrepancy that raises an identity question. Notably, the 1875 San Francisco Great Register entry (src_001) records a Hermann Gatjen aged 21, implying birth ~1854, which is consistent with this index entry; the two may record the same individual. Whether that individual is the same as tree subject I1 requires independent corroboration. The birth year in a passenger index would typically derive from the passenger's self-reported age or a birth year column on the original manifest; neither can be verified without the original.

Prussia is a broad political designation covering a large territory, not a specific locality. It does not identify a German province, town, or parish of origin. The index records no departure port or ship name, so the original manifest — which may carry a more specific origin — cannot be located from this entry alone.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Here is what happened with the two records you asked about.

Both the 1875 San Francisco voter registration (for "Hermann Gatjen") and the Germans to America index entry (for "Herm Gaetjen") give a birth year of about 1854 — one by directly stating it, the other by recording an age of 21 at an 1875 registration.
